chief_complaint: fever, new heart murmur, and vascular skin lesions
hpi_details: A 74-year-old female presents to the clinic with fever, new heart murmur, and vascular skin lesions. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she has a lingering, stubborn strain of the flu or picked up a bug bite while working in her flower garden.
concerns: She is worried that her worsening exhaustion will make it impossible to care for herself at home and force her to move into an assisted living facility.
expectations: She hopes to have blood tests done and leave with a prescription for antibiotics to finally shake off the fever.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Infective Endocarditis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Infective Endocarditis: Draw blood cultures, start IV antibiotics, request echo, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: fever, new heart murmur, and vascular skin lesions

Key HPI features: A 74-year-old female presents to the clinic with fever, new heart murmur, and vascular skin lesions. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.6C, HR 110, BP 108/64. New holosystolic murmur at the apex consistent with mitral regurgitation. Tender erythematous Osler nodes on finger pads, non-tender Janeway lesions on palms, splinter hemorrhages in nail beds. Blood cultures (3 sets) growing Streptococcus viridans. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows a mobile vegetation on the mitral valve.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Infective Endocarditis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Rheumatic fever without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: New murmur with fever — assume endocarditis until proven otherwise.
management_principles: Plan for Infective Endocarditis: Draw blood cultures, start IV antibiotics, request echo
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: fever, new heart murmur, and vascular skin lesions

A 74-year-old female presents to the clinic with fever, new heart murmur, and vascular skin lesions. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 38.6C, HR 110, BP 108/64. New holosystolic murmur at the apex consistent with mitral regurgitation. Tender erythematous Osler nodes on finger pads, non-tender Janeway lesions on palms, splinter hemorrhages in nail beds. Blood cultures (3 sets) growing Streptococcus viridans. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows a mobile vegetation on the mitral valve.
reference_soap.assessment: Infective Endocarditis (mitral valve), meeting Duke criteria with positive blood cultures, echocardiographic vegetation, and peripheral stigmata (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages).
reference_soap.plan: Plan for Infective Endocarditis: Draw blood cultures, start IV antibiotics, request echo. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Infective Endocarditis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Infective Endocarditis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Draw blood cultures, start IV antibiotics, request echo

teaching.one_liner: Bacterial colonization of a heart valve causing fever, a new murmur, and vascular/immunologic skin lesions.
red_flags: New murmur with fever — assume endocarditis until proven otherwise

must_ask.say: How long have you had fevers?
Any recent dental work, IV drug use, or known heart valve problems?
Have you noticed any spots on your skin, palms, or fingers?
Any chest pain or shortness of breath?
Any weight loss or night sweats?

history.answer: I have had a high fever for the past few weeks that will not go away, and I feel completely exhausted.
The fever started about two to three weeks ago and has been gradually getting worse.
My temperature has reached around 38.6 degrees Celsius at home, and I get shaking chills and drenching sweats.
I tried taking acetaminophen, but it only brings my temperature down for an hour or two before the fever spikes back up.
No, I haven't had any cough, sore throat, or runny nose, though I get winded more easily when climbing stairs.
I haven't had any chest pain, but at times my heart feels like it is pounding or racing in my chest.
No burning or pain when I pass urine, no need to go more often, and no pain in my lower back.
No nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or stomach cramps, though I really haven't had much of an appetite.
I have a mild headache whenever the fever goes up, but my neck doesn't feel stiff and I haven't felt confused.
A few days ago I noticed painful red bumps on my fingertips, flat red spots on my palms, and little dark lines under my fingernails.
Yes, I have been waking up drenched in sweat almost every night, and I have lost about three kilograms without trying.
No, I haven't noticed any swollen glands or lumps in my neck, armpits, or groin.
I have not traveled outside the country, spent time in the woods, or been around animals.
No one in my family or close circle has been sick with a fever or any infection.
No, I have never had cancer treatments, chemotherapy, or taken steroid medications.
I had a tooth pulled and a deep dental cleaning about a month ago, but as far as I know I've never had heart valve problems.
No, I haven't started taking any new prescription pills or over-the-counter supplements.
I have never used injected street drugs or shared needles, and I am not currently sexually active.
I have had overwhelming fatigue that makes even simple household tasks feel exhausting.
I thought I just caught a terrible, lingering flu bug or maybe got bitten by an insect while out in my flower garden.
I'm really worried that this exhaustion will keep getting worse until I can no longer live on my own and have to move into a nursing home.
I was hoping to get some blood work done and get a prescription for antibiotics to finally knock out this fever.
I have generally been very healthy and have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart problems.
I have never had surgery or stayed in the hospital, other than delivering my children many years ago.
I do not take any regular prescription medications at all.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine at family gatherings, maybe once a month.
I am retired and live at home with my husband.
My parents lived into their eighties with no history of early heart disease or genetic conditions.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 108/64 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 38.6°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
The patient appears fatigued and flushed, but is alert, oriented, and in no acute distress.
Sclerae are anicteric, with small petechial hemorrhages visible on the palpebral conjunctivae.
No cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy is palpable.
Breath sounds are clear and equal bilaterally, with no wheezes, crackles, or rhonchi.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex radiating to the left axilla.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender throughout without guarding or rigidity.
Mild splenomegaly is palpable just beneath the left costal margin; no hepatomegaly is noted.
No costovertebral angle tenderness is elicited on either side.
Tender erythematous nodules on the finger pads, non-tender erythematous macules on the palms, and splinter hemorrhages in the nail beds.
Neck is supple with full passive range of motion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
